newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: British yachtsman saved in "miracle" rescue.
newsitem.headline: British yachtsman saved in "miracle" rescue.

text.p: British solo sailor Tony Bullimore was plucked from icy seas off the Antarctic on Thursday after miraculously surviving five days inside his upturned yacht.

Captain Raydon Gates, aboard navy frigate HMAS Adelaide, said a "feeling of elation" ran through the ship when Bullimore responded to knocks on the hull of his boat, confirming for the first time since capsizing on Sunday that he was alive.
"Very shortly thereafter he appeared," Gates told Reuters in a telephone interview from the frigate more than 2,500 km from the Australian coast.
"He got out of the yacht himself and appeared just beside the bow of the yacht bobbing away in the waves...Miracle is the word that pops to mind," Gates said.

"It is an absolute Houdini act," said Australian Maritime Safety Authority spokesman David Gray in Canberra where the rescue was co-ordinated. "This is one of the greatest all-time search-and-rescue efforts, there's no doubt about it."

The rescue capped a day of drama in the southern Indian Ocean. Hours earlier, Frenchman Thierry Dubois was winched to safety by a helicopter from the same frigate after drifting in a life raft in heavy seas since Monday.

Gates said 56-year-old Bullimore was "remarkably fit" given his ordeal. Described as a tough former Royal Marine, he was being treated by the ship's doctor for hypothermia and was dehydrated having run out of water two days before his rescue.
He said Bullimore had suffered frostbite on his feet and had lost tip of a finger in an accident.
Dubois, who spent a day clinging to the hull of his upturned yacht before taking to a life raft dropped from the air, was also in surprisingly good health.
The 29-year-old Frenchman was plucked by helicopter from the raft in a "copybook" operation at first light on Thursday after an earlier rescue attempt had been postponed due to bad weather.
Gates said the yachtsman suffered slight hypothermia and had sores on his hands and feet from water exposure.
"His first word was 'Thanks'," Gates said. "He did very little talking but a lot of smiling."
The two sailors were competing in the Vendee Globe round-the-world yacht race, which has justified its reputation as one of the world's most dangerous sporting events.

Another Frenchman in the same race, Raphael Dinelli, was rescued by the Australian navy the day after Christmas and a fourth competitor, Canada's Gerry Roufs, was said on Wednesday to have lost radio contact with race organisers.
Australian Maritime Safety Authority manager search and rescue operations Rick Burleigh said Australia would not be involved in any search for Roufs, who was in Chilean waters.
The rescue brought widespread praise for the defence forces and maritime rescue co-ordination authorities.
"We're proud of them," said Defence Minister Ian McLachlan "There's no doubt that they've all done a marvellous job."
Members of Bullimore's relieved family plan to fly to Australia to greet him when the frigate returns to Perth on Sunday.
Nephew Steven Mulvaney said the yachtsman's family was ecstatic at the succesful rescue and had rarely faltered in their believe that he was alive.

"We have said all the way along that if he was uninjured when the boat turned upside down that there was no reason he couldn't sit quite comfortably in there for any amount of time," he told Australian radio from Bristol.
Navy rescuers had been unable to determine whether Bullimore was alive or even inside his yacht, although a listening device dropped into the water picked up tapping from inside the hull.
Australian Defence Force spokesman Colonel Andrew Reynolds said Bullimore was understood to have survived in the sleeping quarters of his yacht, which held about 145 hours of air.

Gates said Bullimore greeted his rescuers in typically British style. "His first words were 'Thank God' and 'It's a miracle' and when when we got him back on board the ship he said he wouldn't mind a cup of tea," he said.
